# Real-tool wait-hint opportunity evaluation

Authorized: implement and test the workload/environment that exposes useful wait-hint reuse, establish ARC/wait evidence before semantic comparison. Experimental only; preserve previous work and project guards. No deployment.

The application performs actual read-only repository investigations: four live EOS model requests per session and actual search, pytest, evidence commands between them. Model-selected shell is never executed. No artificial tool sleeps, repeated padding, response replay, future tool outputs or future completion times. Tools run without GPU visibility. Both arms receive the same causal hint producer and scheduling configuration; ARC suppresses advice, wait ARC applies it.

Separate offered sessions, client admission and server running-sequence limits. Use server-visible queues for the target test. Continuation scheduling credit is identical in compared arms; it cannot itself be credited to wait hints. Maintain known-prefix advice through first token so a returning request's queue residence does not silently end its protection. Requests retain queued, submitted, tool-complete and first-token clocks. Primary latency includes client admission; HTTP and tool-ready latency are separate.

Initial screens: sixteen distinct source/test investigations, eight server sequences, 1,280 GPU blocks, 1,792 versus 3,584 MiB CPU KV. Hold all other controls fixed, including 8-second continuation credit, pre-tool hints and queue refresh. Follow with a smaller eight-task development profile (four server sequences, 1,024 GPU blocks, 896 MiB CPU KV) to reduce turnaround while retaining actual contention. These sizes are experimental conditions, not an assertion that the largest cache is best. Keep all screens, failures and controls.

Success requires more than allocated VRAM or positive advice counters: observed server queueing, eviction-affected returning prefixes, ready CPU advice, avoided prompt computation, and repeated net workflow throughput or user-visible latency improvement. Different live outputs remain possible and are retained; token rate is not an identical-work causal estimate. Repeat promising profiles in alternating order. Use the larger-cache control to check whether a claimed retention benefit disappears when ARC already retains the working set. Do not manufacture a positive result or reject a technique from an inactive first attempt.

Routine comparisons can opt into compact native output: preserve original runtime audit, transfer/ownership logic, request source counters, cumulative original-prompt work, timings and eviction observations; omit verbose transport/key histories from emitted JSON only. Such records are explicitly not full byte/lifetime proofs. Early full-log runs remain retained. Exact raw tool stdout remains available; an explicit normalization can omit pytest elapsed-time text from the model input, removing irrelevant prompt variation while preserving actual results and counts.

Accounting correction: frontend prefill/external-hit counters describe the first admitted prompt's sources, whereas native execution accumulates scheduled original-prompt work across preemptions and native terminal reuse describes another view. Capture the actual request PrefillStats at first allocation and compare like quantities. Global completed-transfer bytes remain the traffic total; request-attributed bytes need not exhaust it under preemption. Retain their gap rather than equating incompatible counters. Request/prompt/source/preemption identities must agree. Preserve earlier failed accounting checks and their raw timings, without calling those runs validated.

Semantic follow-up: compare ARC, CPU wait-hint ARC, and wait hints composed with existing mean-semantic CPU retention. The semantic arm replaces ARC eviction with the project's SemanticPolicy; it must not be called an ARC-preserving additive policy. Existing semantic-manager advice was inactive because the manager lacked the refresh interface; implement advisory recency without inventing a semantic score, demand hit, session evidence or ownership reference. Require both native relevance updates and CPU refresh, include their cost, preserve exact KV values, and check real-test status claims. No SVD or GPU prefetch claim follows from this arm. Rotate three-way order. Broader answer reasoning remains ungraded.

## Targeted refinement after the first corrected repeat

The 1,280-block/eight-running configuration produced more preemptions with wait advice (32 versus 11), despite much less original-prompt execution. Completed load traffic increased and running-batch occupancy fell. The first pair completed with all source/preemption checks passing, but was slower with wait advice. Stop the remaining confirmation cases with SIGTERM and retained partial records; this is a GPU working-set bottleneck to investigate, not a policy verdict. Test 2,560 GPU blocks at unchanged sixteen sessions, eight running requests and 1,792 MiB CPU budget. This allows more active contexts while remaining below the full offered prefix working set. Check actual eviction/restore/queue activity; a larger allocation alone cannot qualify the environment.

The eight-session compact screen completed with all accounting checks passing, but wait advice did not reduce prompt work or improve token rate/first-token latency. A shorter workflow with fewer generated tokens was not treated as a win. Retain it as a negative operating-point control.

For CPU-only advice, declared wait milliseconds bound acceptance freshness; they do not themselves select a retention duration. A different tool-duration estimator alone cannot fix CPU recency behavior. Queue-time advice, CPU readiness and GPU capacity must be examined directly.


## CPU backing and early protection

At 2,560 GPU blocks but 2,048 CPU blocks, ARC restored no CPU tokens and wait advice restored very few: CPU backing could disappear before the longer-lived GPU prefix. Raising CPU backing to 3,072 blocks produced genuine reuse (38,000 ARC first-admission CPU tokens), no preemptions, and competing CPU evictions. The matched pair was 93.09 versus 92.88 seconds, with average offered first-token latency 6.862 versus 6.595 seconds; this single small difference is not repeatable evidence yet. Both arms completed all sixteen status checks correctly.

The next controlled screen disables only `wait_hint_cpu_retention_gpu_gate` in the wait treatment. In the prior treatment 260 of 393 acknowledged recency calls skipped CPU protection while the complete prefix remained on GPU. The hypothesis is that protecting an already-ready CPU root earlier avoids losing it before GPU eviction. All exact-prefix, ownership, completed-transcript and no-GPU-dispatch guards remain. The default profile is unchanged; this is an explicit experimental configuration. This test changes no tool outputs, offered request count, scheduling credit or memory geometry.


## Fixed three-way comparison

The ungated screen completed with all five accounting identities passing and all 64 responses / 48 actual tools per arm complete. ARC took 93.842 s and wait 87.819 s: +6.86% completed-workflow rate, +7.87% output-token rate, and -0.461 s average offered first-token latency. First-admission computed tokens fell from 56,282 to 49,294; neither arm preempted. This is selection evidence, not independent confirmation.

Freeze the selected operating point for three new rotated ARC/wait/semantic repetitions, using `make bench-agent-pressure` and explicit `semantic_wait_retention_ungated.json`. Mean-semantic retention samples at stride 8. CPU wait control and semantic treatment both protect before GPU eviction. The three-way control override is validated as exact-KV, instrumentation-only ARC with CPU-only advice and no GPU dispatch. Source/tests changed between screen and confirmation to add maintained reporting/intervals/verification; each run retains its own exact corpus and executed source. Do not pool the selecting screen into the confirmation interval.

Primary estimates are paired completed-workflow-rate ratios and average offered first-token differences. Also report output-token rates, output lengths, return/tool-ready latency, physical transfer bytes, preemptions, CPU/GPU memory and power, score updates, CPU refresh and test-status checks. Student-t intervals use whole repetitions, not 64 correlated requests as independent samples. Three repetitions are narrow local evidence; different live generated answers remain a limitation.


## Host-memory and semantic refinement

The first independent fixed-profile pair repeated the selecting result: ARC 94.094 s / offered FTL 7.031 s; wait 88.729 s / 6.590 s. Mean-semantic plus wait activated (12 native applied-score batches, ready CPU refresh), but took 97.50 s / 7.222 s and computed 60,504 prompt tokens versus wait's 49,964. Native source counts agreed, no preemptions, all sixteen status checks correct. This is a measured poor first semantic configuration, not a verdict.

Host diagnostics found 2–3 GiB swap-out per case, with actual tools importing substantial runtime state concurrently; an owned engine/API process inspection also showed swapped host pages. Fast load critical paths do not prove all host memory unaffected. Stop further repetitions using the exact owned supervisor's SIGTERM handler and preserve its first complete three-way comparison plus partial next case. Change the application to four actual subprocess workers while keeping sixteen HTTP sessions/eight server sequences. Queue wait is explicitly recorded; hints continue during real tool-worker queue residence. No artificial sleep is introduced.

Refine semantic retention using existing prefix/chain protection, which avoids making a cached suffix useless by discarding its root, and capture stride 2 to give more opportunities for actual score updates than stride 8. Freeze this configuration for three rotated repetitions. It changes both semantic ranking structure and sampling; if useful, a later ablation would be needed to isolate them. ARC/wait controls share the same bounded tool pool. Do not pool the earlier unbounded-tool results into its interval.


The first bounded-tool pair still showed competing reuse and no preemptions: ARC 106.53 s, wait 99.13 s (+7.47% workflow rate), offered FTL 7.693 versus 7.440 s. CPU prompt execution fell 63,513 to 51,787. Tool-pool wait averaged about four seconds across tools, while pytest execution averaged under ten seconds. Swap-out fell to 368 MiB in the first baseline and about 1 MiB in its wait arm, versus multiple GiB with unbounded tools. Retain this imbalance as a first-run host-state concern and rotate remaining cases; do not declare the complete comparison before repetitions finish.

Refined semantic activated 42 applied-score batches and completed all requests, taking 101.53 s / offered FTL 7.472 s. It narrowed the first configuration's deficit substantially but computed more prompt tokens than wait ARC. The bounded confirmation remains fixed rather than tuning between its repetitions.


## Completed outcome

The final frozen campaign completed all nine rotated cases: 576 successful
responses, 432 actual tools, 144/144 correct reported test statuses and 45/45
native/endpoint identities. Wait/ARC paired workflow throughput +7.00% (95%
interval +5.90% to +8.10%), output-token rate +6.23%, average offered FTL -0.430 s.
Semantic/wait workflow throughput -3.01%; no useful incremental gain was found.
No p95 first-token or VRAM saving claim follows. All nine artifact sets verified
offline, including their unchanged failed/inconclusive statuses. Stop the bounded
hill climb for the reasons in README; broader quality, other real applications,
SVD and GPU prefetch remain outside this comparison. Owned processes reaped,
GPU/locks released, useful evidence and prior-work backups retained.
